messages.subject: Check multi-factor, higher-order, and bi-factor model
messages.subject_clean: Check multi-factor, higher-order, and bi-factor model
messages.body_plain:
Hello, I have a series of question regarding a confirmatory factor analysis.
The factor was measured using a likert-type scale.
Please check the notation of the R syntaxes below and let me know whether it is correct or incorrect. When incorrect, please also let me know how to correct.

I examined the following three models,
a multi-factor model with a syntax for it; Let's call it #model1
a higher-order model with 2 distinct syntaxes for it; Let's call it #model2 and #model3
a bi-factor model with 2 distinct syntaxes for it; Let's call it #model4 and #model5

#model1
m <- 'factor1 =~ the sum of factor1 items
factor2 =~ the sum of factor2 items
factor3 =~ the sum of factor 3 items

factor1 ~~ factor2 + factor3
factor2 ~~ factor3

factor1 ~~ 1*factor1
factor2 ~~ 1*factor2
factor2~~ 1*factor2'

#model2
m <- 'factor1 =~ the sum of factor1 items
factor2 =~ the sum of factor2 items
factor3 =~ the sum of factor 3 items
factor =~ 1*factor1 + 1*factor2+ 1*factor3
factor ~~ factor'

Reference: https://stats.oarc.ucla.edu/r/seminars/rcfa/#s2b

#model3
I also have an alternative higher-order model

m <- 'factor1 =~ the sum of factor1 items
factor2 =~ the sum of factor2 items
factor3 =~ the sum of factor 3 items
factor =~ NA*factor1 + factor2+ factor3
factor ~~ 1*factor'

Reference: https://blogs.baylor.edu/rlatentvariable/sample-page/r-syntax/#Bi-factor_model

#model4
m  <- 'factor1 =~ NA*item 1 and the sum of the factor1 items
factor2 =~ NA*item 2 and the sum of the factor2 items
factor3 =~ NA*item 3 and the sum of the factor3 items
factor =~ NA*item1+ the sum of the factor1-3 items

factor1 =~ 0*factor2+ 0*factor3+ 0*factor
factor2 =~ 0*factor3 + 0*factor
factor3 =~ 0*factor

factor1 ~~ 1* factor1
factor2 ~~ 1* factor2
factor3 ~~ 1* factor3
factor ~~ 1* factor'

Reference: https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2020.01357/full

#model5
I also have an alternative bi-factor model

m  <- 'factor1 =~ the sum of the factor1 items
factor2 =~ the sum of the factor2 items; each factor loading is fixed by a
factor3 =~ the sum of the factor3 items; each factor loading is fixed by b
factor =~ the sum of the factor1-3 items'

Reference: https://blogs.baylor.edu/rlatentvariable/sample-page/r-syntax/#Import_data-3

fit <- cfa(m, data=name, std.lv <http://std.lv>=TRUE)
summary(fit, fit.measures=TRUE, standardized=TRUE)

The reference you take it from gives a specific example where you only have two first-order items. In that case, you need those constraints, but here you have a different case, as you have three first-order factors, so the loadings do not need (or should not, unless you have a good reason to do so) to be constrained to be equal. Therefore, it's better if you estimate them freely and fix the variance of the second-order factor instead, as you do in #model3.

> factor3 =~ NA*item 3 and the sum of the factor3 items

> factor1 =~ 0*factor2+ 0*factor3+ 0*factor
> factor2 =~ 0*factor3 + 0*factor
> factor3 =~ 0*factor
>
> factor1 ~~ 1* factor1
> factor2 ~~ 1* factor2
> factor3 ~~ 1* factor3
> factor ~~ 1* factor'
>
> Reference: https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2020.01357/full

When you want to specify a bi-factor model, what you actually specify is that the factors are "uncorrelated". What you are specifying in the three `factor#=~'  sentences is that left-side factors do not "load" on the right-side one. The correct specification would be:

factor1 ~~ 0*factor2+ 0*factor3+ 0*factor
factor2 ~~ 0*factor3 + 0*factor
factor3 ~~ 0*factor

> #model5
> I also have an alternative bi-factor model
>
> m  <- 'factor1 =~ the sum of the factor1 items
> factor2 =~ the sum of the factor2 items; each factor loading is fixed by a
> factor3 =~ the sum of the factor3 items; each factor loading is fixed by b
> factor =~ the sum of the factor1-3 items'
>
> Reference: https://blogs.baylor.edu/rlatentvariable/sample-page/r-syntax/#Import_data-3

In this case, you are missing the specification that the factors need to be uncorrelated; the specification would be the same as in the previous model:

factor1 ~~ 0*factor2+ 0*factor3+ 0*factor
factor2 ~~ 0*factor3 + 0*factor
factor3 ~~ 0*factor

messages.subject_clean: Error in RI-CLPM when constraining standardised lagged effects
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

I am following Moulder's & Hamaker's syntax to conduct RI-CLPM on 4 variables (E, M, C and y) at 3 time points. The basic model and constraints over time model are working fine, but I'm having trouble with the R script for constraining standardised lagged effects. This is my code:

# RI-CLPM model - constrained standardised lagged effects----
RICLPM6 <- '
  # Create between components (random intercepts)
  RI_E =~ 1*E1 + 1*E2 + 1*E3
  RI_M =~ 1*M1 + 1*M2 + 1*M3
  RI_C =~ 1*C1 + 1*C2 + 1*C3
  RIy =~ 1*y1 + 1*y2 + 1*y3

  # Create within-components with freely estimated factor loadings
  wE1 =~ NA*E1
  wE2 =~ NA*E2
  wE3 =~ NA*E3
  wM1 =~ NA*M1
  wM2 =~ NA*M2
  wM3 =~ NA*M3
  wC1 =~ NA*C1
  wC2 =~ NA*C2
  wC3 =~ NA*C3
  wy1 =~ NA*y1
  wy2 =~ NA*y2
  wy3 =~ NA*y3

  # Estimate lagged effects between within-person centered variables
  # (constrained)
  wy2 ~ a*wE1 + b*wM1 + c*wC1
  wy3 ~ a*wE2 + b*wM2 + c*wC2

  # Label residual covariances
  wy2 ~~ rcov2*wE2
  wy2 ~~ rcov3*wM2
  wy2 ~~ rcov4*wC2
  wy3 ~~ rcov5*wE2
  wy3 ~~ rcov6*wM2
  wy3 ~~ rcov7*wC2

  # Estimate correlation between within-components at first wave
  wy1 ~~ cor1*wE1
  wy1 ~~ cor2*wM1
  wy1 ~~ cor3*wC1

  # Estimate variance and covariance of random intercepts
  RI_E ~~ RI_E
  RIy ~~ RIy
  RIy ~~ RI_E
  RI_M ~~ RI_M
  RI_C ~~ RI_C
  RIy ~~ RI_M
  RIy ~~ RI_C

  # Set variances of within-components at first wave to 1
  wE1 ~~ 1*wE1
  wM1 ~~ 1*wC1
  wC1 ~~ 1*wC1
  wy1 ~~ 1*wy1

  # Label residual variances
  wE2 ~~ rvE2*wE2
  wM2 ~~ rvM2*wM2
  wC2 ~~ rvC2*wC2
  wy2 ~~ rvy2*wy2
  wE3 ~~ rvE3*wE3
  wM3 ~~ rvM3*wM3
  wC3 ~~ rvC3*wC3
  wy3 ~~ rvy3*wy3

  # Constrain grand means over time
  E1 + E2 + E3 ~ mx*1
  M1 + M2 + M3 ~ mz*1
  C1 + C2 + C3 ~ mc*1
  y1 + y2 + y3 ~ my*1

  # Compute correlations of within-components at each wave
  cor2 := a*c + b*c + a*b*cor1 + rcov2
  cor3 := a*c + b*c + a*b*cor2 + rcov3

  # Contrain residual variances of within-components such that variance of each
  # within-component equals 1
  rvE2 == 1 - (a*a + b*b + 2*a*b*cor1)
  rvM2 == 1 - (a*a + b*b + 2*a*b*cor1)
  rvC2 == 1 - (a*a + b*b + 2*a*b*cor1)
  rvy2 == 1 - (c*c + d*d + 2*c*d*cor1)
  rvE3 == 1 - (a*a + b*b + 2*a*b*cor2)
  rvM3 == 1 - (a*a + b*b + 2*a*b*cor2)
  rvC3 == 1 - (a*a + b*b + 2*a*b*cor2)
  rvy3 == 1 - (c*c + d*d + 2*c*d*cor2)
'
RICLPM6.fit <- lavaan(RICLPM6,
                      data = dat1,
                      missing = 'ML',
                      meanstructure = T,
                      int.ov.free = T
)
summary(RICLPM6.fit, standardized = F)
summary(RICLPM6.fit, standardized = T)

And this is the error I'm getting:
Error in lav_start_check_cov(lavpartable = lavpartable, start = START) :
  lavaan ERROR: please provide better fixed values for (co)variances;
                variables involved are: wM1 wC1

I'm not sure where wM1 and wC1 are not working; this nomenclature has been working fine for previous models. Can anyone spot where I'm making an error, please?

Thank you in advance for your help!

Best wishes,
Wika

messages.body_plain:
Hi Kay,

You can read details in the help-page section on Higher-Order Factors.  Basically, your first example isn't modeling a purely higher-order construct because it has both manifest and common-factor indicators.  The formula sort of assumes that a higher-order factor only has common-factor indicators, because that is how the higher-order construct variance is partitioned from the lower-order constructs' error variance and the manifest-variables' error variance.   Calculating the help-page equation manually reveals what is happening:

## common-factor variance using "out1"
(L1 <- lavInspect(out1, "est")$lambda)
(B1 <- lavInspect(out1, "est")$beta)
(P1 <- lavInspect(out1, "est")$psi)
sum(  L1 %*% B1 %*% P1 %*% t(B1) %*% t(L1)  ) # 5.068055

## common-factor variance using "out2"
(L2 <- lavInspect(out2, "est")$lambda)
(B2 <- lavInspect(out2, "est")$beta)
(P2 <- lavInspect(out2, "est")$psi)
sum(  L2 %*% B2 %*% P2 %*% t(B2) %*% t(L2)  ) # 19.90495

Both are expressed relative to the observed total variance of a composite to obtain reliability:

(S <- lavInspect(out1, "sampstat")$cov) # same as out2
sum(S) # 35.31357

So the "out1" version basically ends up "zeroing out" all the common-variance contributions of x7-x9 from Lambda (first-order loadings on "general") because they get multiplied by zero in the Beta matrix (because the lower-order construct "general" does not load on the higher-order construct "general").  Of course, there is only one "general" factor, but that is what I mean about the equation assuming that a higher-order factor is "purely" higher-level, not a blend.  I don't think the 0.144 reliability estimate from out1 is right, because this equation isn't set up to work with factors measured by both manifest and latent indicators.

But the 0.641 you get for "general" from out1 is not right either because without knowing to include the beta matrix, it only accounts for the manifest-indicator contributions (i.e., from x7-x9) to common-factor and total variance:

## or without the higher-order formula
sum(  (L1 %*% P1 %*% t(L1))[7:9, 7:9]  )
## relative to variance of x7-x9 only
sum( S[7:9, 7:9] )
## ratio == 0.641

You want reliability for a composite calculated from x1-x9, not x7-x9.

One solution would be for compRelSEM() to check whether the higher-order factor also has manifest indicators, then change its 0 in the Beta matrix to 1 so it doesn't cancel out the first-order loadings:

B1alt <- B1
B1alt["general", "general"] <- 1
B1alt
## calculate omega
sum(  L1 %*% B1alt %*% P1 %*% t(B1alt) %*% t(L1)  )   /   sum(S) # 0.501

Alternatively, you can already just fit a statistically equivalent CFA that defines x7-x9 as single-indicator constructs, which then load on the higher-order construct.  That will treat "general" as purely higher-order:

HS.model_3 <- '

  visual  =~ x1 + x2 + x3
  textual =~ x4 + x5 + x6

  X7 =~ x7
  X8 =~ x8
  X9 =~ x9
  general =~ visual + textual + X7 + X8 + X9
'
out3 <- cfa(HS.model_3, df) # same df as out1

This yields the same omega estimate as changing Beta above

compRelSEM(out3, higher = "general") # 0.501

So I think 50.1% reliability is the "right" answer for this example.  That is lower than the 56.4% from out2, but out2 is not a statistically equivalent model to out1 and out3.  It is less restrictive (with 1 fewer df), and out2 fits significantly better:

anova(out1, out2)

So we can't expect the estimates to be the same.

messages.subject: Re: invariance testing with categorical data and multiple imputation
messages.subject_clean: invariance testing with categorical data and multiple imputation
messages.body_plain:
Multiple imputation leaves behind a finite degrees of freedom to go into t-tests of individual coefficients and F-tests for multiple coefficients (including model as a whole). Best check with van Buuren's FIMD book https://stefvanbuuren.name/fimd/sec-whyandwhen.html#sec:df -- if you have not read that book, you arguably should not be embarking on multiple imputation projects. The degrees of freedom increase with the number of imputations, and in the worst case it is as low as [# imputations]-1 for the entirely made up data. Historically the magic number of 5 imputations was used for most imputation problems... but then the 1970 estimation problems when Rubin first published this stuff were "estimate regression with five predictors on data set of size n=70", and for those problems 5 imputations would produce 50 degrees of freedom which was OK. Degrees of freedom is a very helpful first step diagnostics that your imputations make any sense. (The subsequent diagnostic steps would include checking distributions -- see https://stefvanbuuren.name/fimd/ch-practice.html, https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/pdf/10.1177/1536867X1201200301, https://doi.org/10.1002/sim.6926.) For SEM models, I would run enough imputations that the imputation degrees of freedom exceed the sample size and exceed twice the model degrees of freedom.

messages.subject: Re: Handling missing data without MCAR
messages.subject_clean: Handling missing data without MCAR
messages.body_plain:
Hi Gabriel,

Whatever you do, you will have to handle the missing data somehow. Listwise deletion (or any other method as far as I am aware) is not better than FIML (listwise is typically one of the worst as it is unbiased only under MCAR). As much as I am aware, proving MCAR/MAR is quite hard and might require additional testing (e.g., interviews to see why people do not respond to some questions). One really useful source I found for decisions on handling missing data is the following: https://doi.org/10.1177/1094428114548590. The key point here is, I believe, to select the "lesser evil" and to also be able to justify why the chosen approach is better than any other.

In lavaan you can use listwise, pairwise and FIML procedures directly. You can also use multiple imputation, but you need another package "survey.lavaan".

I personally routinely use FIML, one of the most optimal and easily implemented methods.

Hope this helps!
Best,
Jošt

messages.body_plain:
Hi, Gabriel,

I was not aware of the "robust.two.stage" option for missing data. In lavaan documentation I found: "Another option (with continuous data) is to use "two.stage" or "robust.two.stage". In this approach, we first estimate the sample statistics (mean vector, variance-covariance matrix) using an EM algorithm. Then, we use these estimated sample statistics as input for a regular analysis (as if the data were complete). The standard errors and test statistics are adjusted correctly to reflect the two-step procedure. The "robust.two.stage" option produces standard errors and a test statistic that are robust against non-normality."

>From this description I would assume that this method uses the expectation-maximization (EM) algorithm, which is, like FIML, based on the maximum likelihood. The paper I suggested also discusses this (EM) approach. In any case, all methods would require some sort of "random missing" assumption. Although, even when data are not missing at random, missing data must be dealt with somehow (and listwise deletion might be the worst option).

By the way, if you have a full SEM (structural and measurement model) and have reflexive measurement instruments then I would personally select FIML. A nice description of how FIML works can be found in C. Enders, 2010, Applied Missing Data Analysis, Chapter 4. This chapter also provides a description of the EM algorithm.

Best,
Jošt

You've created an exactly identified regression problem. Each triplet of the variables at time 1 and time 2 is fully correlated by the virtue of the second set of statements, and all nine cross-covariances are modeled as regression coefficients. You don't need lavaan for this, you would get pretty much the same answer with multivariate regression (multivariate == several outcome variables with the same regressors). The first google search link shows how this works: https://library.virginia.edu/data/articles/getting-started-with-multivariate-multiple-regression. Econometricians had honed that kind of stuff in 1950s (see simultaneous equation models in some older econometrics textbooks; the black Wooldridge "Cross-sectional and Panel Data" is a good universal reference) although they don't have time to teach that stuff anymore, in favor of the causal inference. As such, it would be immaterially different from running OLS / lm() on each equation (there are efficiency gains / smaller standard errors to the extent that the residuals at time 2 are really correlated; if they aren't, the results are equivalent).

This is not to say that this is a good model or a bad model -- as you correctly surmised, you don't have any ability to test the fit, so we cannot really tell. You can drop T2 correlations, but it would only tell you how good the model is in terms of the T2 correlations. If you seriously want to consider different ways to assess your fit, you would want to go back to regression formulation and look at the standard stuff like residual / influence diagnostics.

joh4nd schrieb am Montag, 12. Juni 2023 um 14:28:53 UTC+2:
> @Terrence Jorgensen, do you mind (five years later) expanding a bit on the difference between scaled and robust versions of the fit criteria?
>
> As far as I understand, the criteria labelled "scaled" are old, while the "robust" are new and based in the evidence provided by the two papers by Brosseau-Liard and various colleagues.
>
> Would you agree that the scaled versions are for categorial variables but not necessarily robust estimates, while the robust versions are for robust estimates in general? So that would mean applying any of the below estimators to fit a model would immediately recommend interpreting the robust fitmeasures() described in lavOptions (underlined in the quotation below)?
>
> From lavOptions {lavaan}:
>
> > The estimator to be used. Can be one of the following: "ML" for maximum likelihood, "GLS" for (normal theory) generalized least squares, "WLS" for weighted least squares (sometimes called ADF estimation), "ULS" for unweighted least squares, "DWLS" for diagonally weighted least squares, and "DLS" for distributionally-weighted least squares. These are the main options that affect the estimation. For convenience, the "ML" option can be extended as "MLM", "MLMV", "MLMVS", "MLF", and "MLR". The estimation will still be plain "ML", but now with robust standard errors and a robust (scaled) test statistic. For "MLM", "MLMV", "MLMVS", classic robust standard errors are used (se="robust.sem"); for "MLF", standard errors are based on first-order derivatives (information = "first.order"); for "MLR", ‘Huber-White’ robust standard errors are used (se="robust.huber.white"). In addition, "MLM" will compute a Satorra-Bentler scaled (mean adjusted) test statistic (test="satorra.bentler") , "MLMVS" will compute a mean and variance adjusted test statistic (Satterthwaite style) (test="mean.var.adjusted"), "MLMV" will compute a mean and variance adjusted test statistic (scaled and shifted) (test="scaled.shifted"), and "MLR" will compute a test statistic which is asymptotically equivalent to the Yuan-Bentler T2-star test statistic (test="yuan.bentler.mplus"). Analogously, the estimators "WLSM" and "WLSMV" imply the "DWLS" estimator (not the "WLS" estimator) with robust standard errors and a mean or mean and variance adjusted test statistic. Estimators "ULSM" and "ULSMV" imply the "ULS" estimator with robust standard errors and a mean or mean and variance adjusted test statistic.
>
> Regards,
> Johan

Hello all,

I am attempting to estimate a multiple indicator RI-CLPM in which I request FIML.x for missing and specify a panel sample weight using sampling.weights. The specifics of the call are:

its.riclpm.fl.weak.si.fit2 <- lavaan(its.riclpm.fl.weak.si <http://its.riclpm.fl.weak.si>,data=itsdata, estimator="MLR",missing="FIML.x",sampling.weights = "t7finwt")

I've received the following error message:
Error in stats::cov.wt(RAW, wt = wt[Mp$case.idx[[p]]], method = "ML") : weights must be non-negative and not all zero
I checked the weights, and none are negative, and they are not all zero. That said, about 67% of the weights are zero because of attrition. I came across a recent post on Stack Overflow where someone is having a similar issue, but there has not been an answer provided yet.

https://stackoverflow.com/questions/77626343/using-fiml-with-sample-weights-in-lavaan-with-fixed-x-f

Any insights are much appreciated. Thank you.

Best,

Ryan

messages.body_plain:
I'd say you may have either of the following two issues (or some combination of both):
You have a large n, so when weights are normalised (i.e. so that they sum up to 1), they all get so small they become "computational zeros".
Your valid cases (the ones actually being used to fit the model) all have a zero weight value.
Not really sure how to solve it; without a reprex one can experiment with it's difficult to find a solution, but you can try filtering out the cases with a zero-weight and see what happens. It may not be the optimal solution but it can point you in the right direction.

Hope it helps,
Daniel

Sorry yes that is user defined but it simply outputs the model syntax, based on the RI_CLPM structure described here https://jeroendmulder.github.io/RI-CLPM/lavaan.html for example

I pasted the function here for reference (highlighted in red the portion where I set the equality constraints I want to weight

So for example if you now call
f = riclpm_formula('x', 'y', meas_time=list(c(3, 4.5, 5.2), c(2.9, 4.4, 6)))
it should print out an example where x was measured at 3, 4.5, and 5.2 years and y was measured at 2.9, 4.4, and 6 years.

riclpm_formula <- function(var1='dep', var2='cmr',
                                                n_ocs=NULL, meas_time=list(c(), c()),
                                                stationarity=TRUE,
                                                verbose=TRUE) {

  # Check input ----------------------------------------------------------------
  if (is.null(n_ocs) & (length(meas_time[[1]])==0 | length(meas_time[[1]])==0)) {
    stop('Provide total number of occasions or time points of measurement!') }

  if (length(meas_time[[1]]) != length(meas_time[[2]])) {
    stop('You need the same number of time points for each of the two variables.') }

  if (!is.null(n_ocs) & !length(meas_time[[1]]) %in% c(0, n_ocs)) { # contraddictory info
    stop('Number of occations and measurement times provided do not agree.') }

  # ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
  # How many occasions
  if (length(meas_time[[1]]) > 0) {
    temp_var1 = meas_time[[1]]
    temp_var2 = meas_time[[2]]
  } else {
    temp_var1 = temp_var2 = 1:n_ocs
  }

  if (is.null(n_ocs)) { n_ocs = length(temp_var1) }

  # Create between components (random intercepts)
  random_intercepts = paste0('# Random intercepts\n',
                             'ri_',var1,' =~ ', paste0('1*',var1,1:n_ocs, collapse=' + '), '\n',
                             'ri_',var2,' =~ ', paste0('1*',var2,1:n_ocs, collapse=' + '), '\n')

  # Create within-components (or within-person centered variables)
  # Note: factor loadings are set to 1 in non-stationary model and freely estimated in stationary models
  if (stationarity) { l = 'NA*' } else { l = '1*' }

  impulses = paste0('# Impulses\n',
                    paste0('w_',var1,1:n_ocs,' =~ ',l,var1,1:n_ocs, collapse='\n'), '\n',
                    paste0('w_',var2,1:n_ocs,' =~ ',l,var2,1:n_ocs, collapse='\n'), '\n')

  # Estimate lagged effects between within-person centered variables
  regressions = '# Regressions\n'
  for (i in 2:n_ocs) {
    # if (n_strata > 1) { ... ar_1 <- paste0('c(', paste0(rep(paste0('AR_',var1,i-1),strata), collapse=', '), ')') #define  strata

    ar_1 <- paste0('AR_',var1,i-1)
    ar_2 <- paste0('AR_',var2,i-1)
    cl_1 <- paste0('CL_',var1,i-1)
    cl_2 <- paste0('CL_',var2,i-1)

    regressions = paste0(regressions,
      'w_',var1,i,' ~ ',ar_1,' * w_',var1,i-1,' + ',cl_1,' * w_',var2,i-1,'\n',
      'w_',var2,i,' ~ ',ar_2,' * w_',var2,i-1,' + ',cl_2,' * w_',var1,i-1,'\n')
  }

  # Estimate covariance between within-person centered variables
  covariances = paste0('# Covariances\n',
                       # Estimate correlation between within-components at first wave
                       'w_',var1,'1 ~~ cor1 * w_',var2,'1\n',

                       # Estimate residual covariances (between residuals of within-person vars, i.e., innovations)
                       paste0('w_',var1,2:n_ocs,' ~~ rcov',2:n_ocs,' * w_',var2,2:n_ocs, collapse='\n'), '\n',

                       # Estimate covariance of the random intercepts
                       'ri_',var1,' ~~ covRI * ri_',var2,'\n')

  if (stationarity) { w1 = '1*' } else { w1 = '' }

  variances = paste0('# Variances\n',
                     # Set variances of within-components at first wave to 1
                     paste0('w_',var1,'1 ~~ ',w1,'w_',var1,'1\n', 'w_',var2,'1 ~~ ',w1,'w_',var2,'1\n'),

                     # Estimate (and label) residual variances of within-person centered variables
                     paste0('w_',var1,2:n_ocs,' ~~ rvar_',var1,2:n_ocs,'*w_',var1,2:n_ocs, collapse='\n'),'\n',
                     paste0('w_',var2,2:n_ocs,' ~~ rvar_',var2,2:n_ocs,'*w_',var2,2:n_ocs, collapse='\n'),'\n',

                     # Estimate variance of random intercepts
                     'ri_',var1,' ~~ ri_',var1,'\nri_',var2,' ~~ ri_',var2, '\n')

  constraints = ar_var1_con = ar_var2_con = cl_var1_con = cl_var2_con = cor_con = rvar_con = ''

  if (stationarity) {
    constraints = '# Constraints\n'

    # paste0('# Constrain grand means over time\n',
    # paste0(var1,1:n_ocs, collapse=' + '), ' ~ mean_',var1,'*1\n',
    # paste0(var2,1:n_ocs, collapse=' + '), ' ~ mean_',var2,'*1\n')

    # Weight for unequal temporal gaps
    rel='^' # '*'
    i = 1:(n_ocs-2) # iterator
    prec=2 # precision
    # NOTE: round to nearest integer for the moment
    ar_var1_con <- paste0('AR_',var1,i,rel,round(temp_var1[i+1]-temp_var1[i], prec), ' == AR_',var1,i+1,rel,round(temp_var1[i+2]-temp_var1[i+1], prec),
                          collapse='\n')
    ar_var2_con <- paste0('AR_',var2,i,rel,round(temp_var2[i+1]-temp_var2[i], prec), ' == AR_',var2,i+1,rel,round(temp_var2[i+2]-temp_var2[i+1], prec),
                          collapse='\n')
    cl_var1_con <- paste0('CL_',var1,i,rel,round(temp_var1[i+1]-temp_var2[i], prec), ' == CL_',var1,i+1,rel,round(temp_var1[i+2]-temp_var2[i+1], prec),
                          collapse='\n')
    cl_var2_con <- paste0('CL_',var2,i,rel,round(temp_var2[i+1]-temp_var1[i], prec), ' == CL_',var2,i+1,rel,round(temp_var2[i+2]-temp_var1[i+1], prec),
                          collapse='\n')

    # Compute correlations between the within-components themselves at each wave
    i = 1:(n_ocs-1) # new iterator
    cor_con <- paste0('cor',2:n_ocs, ' := AR_',var1,i,'*CL_',var2,i,' + ', 'CL_',var1,i,'*AR_',var2,i,' + ',
                                                                  'AR_',var1,i,'*AR_',var2,i,'*cor',i,' + ', 'CL_',var1,i,'*CL_',var2,i,'*cor',i,' + rcov',2:n_ocs, collapse='\n')

    # Constrain residual variances of within-components such that the total variance of each
    # within-component equals 1
    rvar_con <- paste0('rvar_',var1,2:n_ocs,' == 1 - (AR_',var1,i,'*AR_',var1,i,' + ', 'CL_',var1,i,'*CL_',var1,i,' + 2*AR_',var1,i,'*CL_',var1,i,'*cor',i,')\n',
                                      'rvar_',var2,2:n_ocs,' == 1 - (AR_',var2,i,'*AR_',var2,i,' + ', 'CL_',var2,i,'*CL_',var2,i,' + 2*AR_',var2,i,'*CL_',var2,i,'*cor',i,')', collapse = '\n')
  }

  constraints = paste0(constraints, ar_var1_con,'\n', ar_var2_con,'\n', cl_var1_con,'\n', cl_var2_con, '\n', cor_con,'\n',rvar_con)

  f = paste0(random_intercepts, impulses, regressions, covariances, variances, constraints)

  if (verbose) { cat(f) }

  return(f)
}

messages.subject: Model comparison using binary data
messages.subject_clean: Model comparison using binary data
messages.body_plain:
I am analysing a questionnaire for which solutions with different numbers of factors (ranging from 3-9) have been identified in the literature. The questionnaire has 72 binary Yes/No responses.

I have quite a large sample (N = 2400), so I have split the sample into an EFA discovery sample, and a CFA validation sample. I used EFA to generate model structures ranging from 1-9 factors, and then want to compare them in the CFA data. Each model has the same items.

My questions are about comparing the models in the CFA dataset. As I understand it, the models are not nested (I cannot reduce the higher dimensinoality models to the lower ones by parametric constraints), which limits direct comparison with change in RMSEA. I would normally compare models like this using AIC or BIC, which has the advantage of penalizing model complexity. To get AIC/BIC, I need to use a ML-based estimator.

I first ran this using FIML on the polychoric correlation matrices estimated for the validation sample. However, I realise on further reading that this is flawed as it treats the polychoric correlations as observed rather than estimated (See exchange below from another conversation (https://groups.google.com/g/lavaan/c/aIM6A5fd9NQ/m/LTbdA4tpAQAJ)

“I had the (maybe stupid?) idea of using using lavCov() to create a polychoric covariance matrix that I then can use as an input for ML estimation

You can't trust the SEs or test statistics because they treat the polychorics as known observations rather than as estimates (with their own SEs).  Taking the uncertainty of the first-step estimates into account is what DWLS does.”

My questions:

1)  So is it sensible to run this using the MLR estimator on the observed data, which would treat them as numerical and continuous?

I understand this runs the risk of underestimating the factor loadings, but does it bias estimates of AIC/BIC? Would this be dependent on the number of factors e.g. would it bias models with more/fewer factors, thus making the analysis not very useful?

2) Is there any better way of comparing non-nested models of binary data with varying numbers of factors but the same underlying items?

3) To get unbiased factor loading estimates, I will estimate the winning model with a DWLS estimator on 25 multiply imputed datasets. Does this risk that a model that would perform better with an estimator appropriate for categorical data, would have been rejected earlier on by the MLR model comparison?

Thanks very much for any thoughts!

Dan

messages.body_plain:
Product indicators are poor man's approximations in measurement models from 1990s. In 2023, I would do Bayesian / RStan. You can code absolutely anything in terms of how the latent variables relate to one another, and absolutely anything in terms of measurement -- especially if any of the indicators are Likert scale. The marginal effects would require a tad more coding depending on the point at which you are evaluating them -- as the model is nonlinear, these effects will differ from point to point of the Xa and Ya space.

Of course doing Bayesian correctly is its own layer of computational statistics. But for early career researchers, it is very much worth figuring out.

head(d)

I do not yet know the source of the problem but I guess it is due to the model, not the ability of lavaan to handle noninteger exponents. I can fit Terrence's model using the CRAN version of lavaan (0.6.16). I call sem() instead of lavaan() because there may be some preset values that we need sem() to handle. Calling lavaan() is error prone because we may forget to set those values, resulting in a model different from what we expect. There are rarely cases in which there are things that can be done only by calling lavaan() but not by calling sem() (except for refitting a models using internal slots, as in some packages).

In the example above, if I run the following, with mod being the full model in the first post:

m <- lavaan::lavaan( mod,
                      data = dat,

                      se = 'robust',
                      missing = 'fiml', # group = group,
                      meanstructure = TRUE,
                      int.ov.free = TRUE)

I got this error:

Error in sigma.inv * TT : non-conformable arrays

Not sure if this can help but you can try to add verbose = TRUE to see where the estimation failed. If I run the following using the random data:

m0 <- lavaan::sem(mod,
                  data = dat,
                  meanstructure = TRUE,
                  verbose = TRUE)

The failure occurred at attempt 4:

attempt 4 -- optim.parscale = "standardized" + start = "simple"

In your case using your real data, the output may be different. In any case, the printout may give some hints on the source of the failure.in <http://failure.in> estimation.

You can also fit a simpler model with only three waves, and see whether the problem still occurs. If estimation still fails quickly, it may be easier to diagnose the problem using a three-wave model.

Hope this helps.

-- Shu Fai

Hi, Dan,

My colleagues and I are conducting a study about model selection.
The results are still preliminary, and hopefully the final version will be published in the second semester of 2024, but one thing that hasn't changed since the beginning is that treating ordinal items as ordinal or intervalar makes little difference in the goodness-of-fit indexes. So, there should be no problem in using the MLR estimator to get AIC/BIC and select the best model.
However, if you do want precise estimations of the factor loadings, then after selecting the best model, you have to repeat the analysis using DWLS estimator.

Hope this helps,
Yago

Dear all,

A new update of lavaan (0.6.17) is now available on CRAN. This release
fixes the following bugs/issues:

- efa() did not work with sample.cov= (instead of data=)

- group.equal= did not work properly in multigroup-multilevel models

- summary(fit, rsquare = TRUE) failed in some settings

- lavTestScore() + epc = TRUE produced epc values with the wrong sign if
the estimator was not ML

- factor scores for categorical data were not correctly scaled when
parameterization = “theta”

- in 0.6-16 only: multilevel results were sometimes slightly off, if
some variables were within-only

- lav_data_update_subset() (only used in sam()) did not recompute @nobs
if empty cases were present in (the subset of) the data

New features and user-visible changes:

- summary() and parameterEstimates() will now (per default) remove
unused rows corresponding to parameters that are automatically added,
but still fixed to their default values; add remove.unused = FALSE to
get them back

This is most visible when data is categorical: the fixed-to-zero
intercepts and the fixed-to-one scaling factors are no longer printed by
default.

- the default arguments of the sem/cfa/growth function (for example
int.ov.free, int.lv.free) can now be changed when using the
sem/cfa/growth functions

This implies that you can use (say) sem(model, data = Data,
meanstructure = TRUE, int.ov.free = FALSE, int.lv.free = TRUE),
overwriting the default setting of the sem() function.

- requesting estimator = “WLSMV” (or “DWLS”) without categorical data
now produces a warning

- estimator = “PML” now supports sampling weights (thanks to Haziq Jamil)

- modindices() now warns if equality constraints are involved

- lavPredict() gains a mdist= argument to compute casewise Mahalanobis
distances for factor scores and/or casewise residualss

The latter allows to create a diagnostic plot not unlike the plots shown
in Yuan & Hayashi (2010). The function below (not included in lavaan
yet, based on code written by Maxwell Mansolf) illustrates how this can
be done as a proof-of-concept.

Yves.

lavPlotDiagnostics <- function(lavobject, type = "mdist.fs.resid", block
= 1L,
                                alpha = 0.01, nlabel = 5L, ...) {

     type <- tolower(type)
     if(!type %in% c("mdist.fs.resid", "qchi.mdist.resid")) {
         stop("lavaan ERROR: type= must be mdist.fs.resid or
qchi.mdist.resid")
     }

     lavmodel <- lavobject@Model

     if(type == "mdist.fs.resid") {

         # Bartlett factor scores
         out.fs <- lavPredict(lavobject, type = "lv", method = "Bartlett",
                              mdist = TRUE, drop.list.single.group = FALSE)
         mdist.fs <- sqrt(attr(out.fs, "mdist")[[block]])
         nfac <- ncol(out.fs[[block]])

         # casewise residuals
         out.resid <- lavPredict(lavobject, type = "resid", method =
"Bartlett",
                              mdist = TRUE, drop.list.single.group = FALSE)
         mdist.resid <- sqrt(attr(out.resid, "mdist")[[block]])
         nvar <- ncol(out.resid[[block]])

         # critical values
         df.fs <- nfac
         df.resid <- nvar - nfac
         qf <- sqrt(qchisq((1 - alpha), df.fs))
         qr <- sqrt(qchisq((1 - alpha), df.resid))

         # scatter plot
         XLIM <- range(c(mdist.fs[   is.finite(mdist.fs)],    qf)) *
c(1,1.05)
         YLIM <- range(c(mdist.resid[is.finite(mdist.resid)], qr)) *
c(1,1.05)
         plot(mdist.fs, mdist.resid,
              xlim = XLIM, ylim = YLIM,
              xlab = "M-distance factor scores (leverage)",
              ylab = "M-distance casewise residuals (outliers)",
              ...)

         # critical lines
         abline(v = qf)
         abline(h = qr)

         # add points close to the line
         qr2 <- qr - 0.05
         qf2 <- qf - 0.05
         # bottom right: leverage points (but not outliers)
         idx <- which(mdist.fs >= qf2 & mdist.resid < qr2)
         if(length(idx) > 0L) {
             text(x = mdist.fs[idx], mdist.resid[idx],
                  labels = as.character(idx), pos = 4L, col = "darkgreen")
         }

         # top left: potential outliers (but not leverage observations)
         idx <- which(mdist.resid >= qr2 & mdist.fs < qf2)
         if(length(idx) > 0L) {
             text(x = mdist.fs[idx], mdist.resid[idx],
                  labels = as.character(idx), pos = 4L, col = "darkgreen")
         }

         # top right: both outliers and leverage points
         idx <- which(mdist.fs >= qf2 & mdist.resid >= qr2)
         if(length(idx) > 0L) {
             text(x = mdist.fs[idx], mdist.resid[idx],
                  labels = as.character(idx), pos = 4L, col = "red")
         }
     } # type = "mdist.fs.resid"

     else if(type == "qchi.mdist.resid") {

         # Bartlett factor scores
         out.fs <- lavPredict(lavobject, type = "lv", method = "Bartlett",
                              mdist = TRUE, drop.list.single.group = FALSE)
         # mdist.fs <- sqrt(attr(out.fs, "mdist")[[block]])
         nfac <- ncol(out.fs[[block]])

         # casewise residuals
         out.resid <- lavPredict(lavobject, type = "resid", method =
"Bartlett",
                              mdist = TRUE, drop.list.single.group = FALSE)
         mdist.resid <- sqrt(attr(out.resid, "mdist")[[block]])
         nvar <- ncol(out.resid[[block]])

         # sort casewise residuals
         out <- sort.int <http://sort.int>(mdist.resid, index.return = TRUE)
         mdist.resid.sorted <- out$x

         # (squared) chisq quantiles
         qq <- sqrt(qchisq(ppoints(length(mdist.resid)), df = nvar - nfac))

         # scatter plot
         XLIM <- range(qq) * c(1, 1.05)
         YLIM <- range(mdist.resid[is.finite(mdist.resid)]) * c(1, 1.05)
         plot(qq, mdist.resid.sorted,
              xlim = XLIM, ylim = YLIM,
              xlab = "Quantiles of (squared) chi-squared distribution",
              ylab = "M-distance casewise residuals (outliers)",
              ...)

         # label 'nlabel' largest residuals
         N <- length(mdist.resid.sorted)
         x.idx <- (N - nlabel + 1L):N
         y.idx <- out$ix[x.idx]
         if(nlabel > 0L) {
             text(x = qq[x.idx], y = mdist.resid[y.idx],
                  labels = as.character(y.idx), pos = 3L)
         }
     } # plot == qchi.mdist.resid

On 11/23/23 11:08, J Pap wrote:
> reg <- '
>          #measurement
>           Predicted =~Z1 + Z2 + Z3
>           Xa=~X1+ X2
>           Ya=~Y1+ Y2
>           #path
>           Predicted ~  Xa + Ya + I(Xa^2) + Xa*Ya
>    '
> Reg_fit<- sem(reg, data = dat, estimator = "MLR")

The sam() function (in 0.6-17) can handle second-order terms (i.e.
quadratic terms and product terms) for latent predictors, but using a
different syntax:

Predicted ~  Xa + Ya + Xa:Xa + Xa:Ya

(You will have to put Xa and Ya in a single measurement block, as they
only have 2 indicators). A paper about this is under review. That is why
this feature is not 'official' yet. But it will not help you with the
marginal effects.

Another approach (to get the marginal effects) is to use the Skrondal
and Laake (2001) approach: compute 'Bartlett' factor scores for the
dependent variable (here: Predicted) and 'regression' factor scores for
the two (latent) predictors together. Once you have these 'observed'
values, you can proceed as in ordinary regression. See:

Ng, J. C., & Chan, W. (2020). Latent moderation analysis: A factor score
approach. Structural Equation Modeling: A Multidisciplinary Journal, 27
(4), 629–648.

Yves.

On 12/21/23 13:36, Ariadna Albajara Sáenz wrote:

> I have a 4-point 4-item scale, however I have some missing data and I

> cfa (specified_model, data = nameofdataset, std.lv <http://std.lv> = F, meanstructure =
> T, ordered = TRUE) OR
> I read a paper from Lei et al. 2019 recommending using MLR-CAT in case

> https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/10705511.2019.1680292
> <https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/10705511.2019.1680292>?
> What would you recommend?

If the amount of missing data is small, and you can assume MCAR, then
WLSMV + pairwise deletion is usually ok.

Full casewise ML (FIML), treating the variables as categorical is
probably superior, but not available in lavaan. (Maybe in IRT packages?)

But if the 4-point scales are reasonably symmetric, you may get
reasonable results if you treat the data as continuous, and you use
estimator = "MLR" in combination with missing = "ml" (=fiml)

> Question 2: CONTINOUS
> For continuous variables (5-point 6 item scale), is it necessary to
> indicate missing = "fiml" when using estimator = "MLR" or does MLR uses
> fiml by default?

You need to explicitly set missing = "fiml".

Yves.
